title: Branch Profitability
summary: Branch EBITDA or contribution margin after local costs.
whyPeCares: PE cares because this KPI gives an early read on growth quality, margin expansion, cash conversion, execution discipline, or exit-story credibility.
goodBadSignals: Good performance shows controlled execution and improving unit economics; bad performance signals leakage, weak process ownership, or a diligence risk requiring deeper segmentation.
improvementActions: Standardize the definition and data owner.
Segment by customer, site, product, team, or channel.
Tie movement to an operating playbook and weekly cadence.

articleSections.title: Defining the Multi-Unit Economic Model
body: Branch Profitability is the cornerstone of value creation in multi-site platform investments, representing the fundamental unit of economic truth. For an operating partner, the 'Branch' is the laboratory where the investment thesis is either validated or dismantled. We define this as the Fully Burdened Operating Income generated by a specific geographic or logical unit, after accounting for all direct costs and a proportional share of regional overhead.

To calculate true branch-level performance, we apply a strict 'Contribution Margin' framework: (Branch Revenue - COGS - Direct Labor - Facility Costs - Local Marketing). The math must be granular; for instance, if a HVAC services branch generates $500k in monthly revenue with a 40% gross margin, but carries $150k in fixed facility and local admin costs, its Branch EBITDA is $50k (10%). We look for 'High-Performance Outliers' that exceed the 15% threshold to identify scalable best practices.

We utilize Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) tools like NetSuite or Sage Intacct to segment P&Ls by 'Location' dimensions. This allows for automated, real-time variance analysis against the 'Model Branch' profile. Without this level of digital visibility, management is flying blind, relying on lagging indicators rather than the leading drivers of unit-level cash flow.
articleSections.callout: In private equity, we don't buy companies; we buy a collection of branch-level P&Ls. If you can't fix the unit, you can't fix the platform.

articleSections.title: The Four Levers of Branch Optimization
body: Optimizing branch performance requires a surgical focus on four distinct levers: Revenue Density, Labor Productivity, Fixed Cost Leverage, and Local Market Pricing. Revenue Density is the most critical in service businesses; by increasing the number of jobs within a 20-mile radius of the branch, we drastically reduce 'Windshield Time' (unbilled travel), directly boosting the billable hour per technician ratio.

Labor Productivity is measured via the 'Revenue per FTE' metric, which we benchmark across the entire portfolio. For a dental platform, if the top decile branches produce $400k per chair while the bottom decile produces $250k, the delta represents the 'Value Gap'. We implement 'Standard Operating Procedures' (SOPs) and performance-based incentive programs to bridge this gap, often utilizing workforce management tools like Deputy or UKG.

Fixed Cost Leverage is the 'Operating Leverage' play. As a branch scales from $2M to $5M in revenue, the facility rent and base admin costs should remain relatively static, allowing incremental margins to flow directly to the bottom line. We track the 'Incremental EBITDA Margin'—aiming for 25% or higher on every dollar of growth above the branch breakeven point.

articleSections.title: Variance Analysis and the 'Red Zone' Protocol
body: Continuous monitoring via 'Heat Maps' is essential for identifying underperforming units before they erode platform-level covenants. We categorize branches into 'Performance Tiers': Tier 1 (Self-Sustaining), Tier 2 (Growth Target), and Tier 3 (Turnaround). Any branch falling below 80% of its EBITDA budget for two consecutive months triggers the 'Red Zone' protocol, involving a mandatory onsite operational audit.

The math of the turnaround involves a 'Zero-Based Budgeting' exercise at the branch level. If a branch is losing money, we analyze the 'Breakeven Revenue' requirement: Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin %. For a retail clinic with $80k in monthly fixed costs and a 60% margin, the breakeven is $133k. If current revenue is $110k, the operator must decide between a 20% volume increase or a drastic cost restructuring.

Modern BI tools like Tableau or PowerBI are used to overlay financial data with operational 'Leading Indicators' like Lead-to-Close ratios and Technician Utilization. If a branch's profitability is declining despite high utilization, it usually indicates a 'Pricing Leakage' or 'Material Waste' issue that requires immediate field-level intervention.

articleSections.title: Scaling Through 'De Novo' and Bolt-on Integration
body: The 'Branch Playbook' is the blueprint for non-organic growth. When opening a 'De Novo' (new) location, we follow a strict 'Capital Allocation' model: Target ROIC of >30% by Year 3. This requires a disciplined ramp-up phase where the 'Negative Cash Flow' period is strictly managed through centralized procurement and standardized hiring templates.

For 'Bolt-on' acquisitions, the 'Integration Margin' is the primary goal. We typically acquire independent operators at a 4-6x EBITDA multiple and, through branch-level synergies (consolidating back-office, better vendor pricing, cross-selling), we drive them toward the platform's 10-12x exit multiple. The math is simple: a $1M EBITDA acquisition transformed into a $1.5M EBITDA branch through operational rigor creates massive shareholder value.

Tools like Asana or Smartsheet are used to manage the '100-Day Integration Plan' for every new branch. We track 'Synergy Capture' in real-time, ensuring that the 'Day 1' P&L is quickly aligned with the platform's 'Chart of Accounts' and operational benchmarks.

articleSections.title: Exit Readiness and Unit Economic Proof
body: When preparing for an exit, the 'Quality of Earnings' (QofE) report will scrutinize branch-level consistency. A buyer wants to see that profitability is not dependent on a few star performers but is a result of a 'Systematized Process'. We prepare 'Cohort Analysis' reports showing that even newer branches are achieving target margins within the expected timeframe.

We calculate the 'LTV to CAC' ratio at the branch level to prove the long-term viability of the customer base. If a branch has a high churn rate or low customer lifetime value, it suggests local market saturation or poor service quality. A healthy branch should maintain an LTV/CAC ratio above 3x, signifying a highly efficient 'Customer Acquisition Engine'.

The final 'Exit Deck' must present the 'Branch Bridge'—a waterfall chart showing how the platform moved from an average 8% branch margin at entry to 14% at exit. This narrative, backed by granular, auditable data from the ERP, is what drives the 'Multiple Expansion' that private equity firms crave.
